Pre-requisite: Familiarity with text preprocessing techniques. Some experience with ML/DL libraries

Course Objective
The aim of this course is to provide students with foundational knowledge in Natural Language
Processing (NLP), including text processing, classification, and deep learning models like CNNs and
RNNs. Students will apply transfer learning for NLP tasks and explore voice recognition systems. By
the end, they will be prepared to implement NLP solutions across fields like healthcare, finance, and
technology.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Understand the core components of NLP and explain their applications across various real-
world contexts.
2. Analyze and implement text classification techniques to address specific NLP tasks effectively.
3. Apply deep learning methods, including CNNs and RNNs, to tackle advanced NLP
challenges.
4. Evaluate and adapt transfer learning techniques to enhance model performance and versatility
across NLP applications.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge on types of application architecture
Course Objective
This course equips students with the skills to architect and deploy AI applications using monolithic
and microservices architectures, Kubernetes, APIs, and MLOps principles. It emphasizes hands-on
experience with containerization, Docker, and orchestration tools for scalable AI deployment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Compare and contrast monolithic and microservices architectures, evaluating their
advantages and disadvantages in the context of AI applications.
2. Demonstrate the use of Kubernetes for managing and deploying AI models in production,
explaining its key concepts and functionality.
3. Apply MLOps principles, including data preparation, model deployment, and monitoring,
to optimize the end-to-end machine learning lifecycle.
4. Evaluate and implement containerization techniques using Docker and Kubernetes,

Pre-requisite: NA
Course Objective
This course introduces students to the principles of building secure AI applications, emphasizing
responsible AI practices, data privacy, and cybersecurity compliance. Students will explore techniques
to secure AI application deployment and usage, understand regulatory requirements like GDPR, and
apply privacy-preserving methods. By course end, they will be equipped to design, secure, and ethically
manage AI systems in diverse domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Apply Responsible AI principles to design and implement AI applications effectively.
2. Analyze and implement security measures to safeguard AI application deployments.
3. Evaluate and apply techniques for ensuring secure usage and operation of AI applications.
4. Design a compliance audit framework tailored for an AI system, ensuring it addresses key
regulatory requirements and mitigates identified risks.

Course Objective
The Seminar course is designed to enhance the students' presentation and research skills. It provides
students an opportunity to explore contemporary topics in data science, conduct an in-depth literature
review, and present their findings to an academic audience. The seminar aims to develop critical
thinking, oral communication, and the ability to engage with technical discussions.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Identify and evaluate recent advancements or research trends in a chosen domain of data science
through comprehensive literature review.
2. Develop and deliver clear, concise technical presentations with effective oral communication
skills.
3. Synthesize research findings into a structured, well-documented technical report.
4. Demonstrate the ability to address technical questions and engage in meaningful discussions
during presentations.
Detailed Syllabus
The students of a group would contact the concerned faculty to find a mutually convenient 2 hour/
week schedule for the seminar course. The group would be required to meet their faculty instructor
regularly and seek advice on the topic of the seminar and guidance in various aspects of technical
presentation (Example: Composition of presentation, Length of presentation, Graphical Vs textual
aspects, Content density, etc.) The organization of the course can be divided into two parts. The initial
phase includes the students deciding seminar topics and receiving guidance on technical
communication aspects. This could also include mock presentations which could facilitate faculty and
peer feedback. The second part of the seminar course would include student presentations, spread over
several sessions; based on which grade is awarded.

models like GANs, VAEs, and transformers. Additionally, the course addresses prompt engineering
and ethical considerations in AI, such as bias and transparency.

1. Understand the fundamental concepts of neural networks, including architectures, training
algorithms, and optimization techniques

neural networks (RNNs)
3. Apply generative models such as generative adversarial networks (GANs), variational
autoencoders (VAEs), and transformers

2. Analyze and implement security measures to safeguard AI application deployments.
3. Evaluate and apply techniques for ensuring secure usage and operation of AI applications.
4. Design a compliance audit framework tailored for an AI system, ensuring it addresses key

Pre requisite: Nil
Course Objective
Computer Vision focuses on the development of algorithms and techniques to analyze and
interpret the visible world around us. This requires understanding of the fundamental concepts
related to multi-dimensional signal processing, feature extraction, pattern analysis, visual
geometric modelling, stochastic optimization etc. Knowledge of these concepts is necessary in
this field, to explore and contribute to research and further developments in the field of computer
vision. Applications range from Biometrics, Medical diagnosis, document processing, mining of
visual content, to surveillance, advanced rendering etc. The aim of the course is to familiarize
the students with the fundamental concepts of Computer Vision. It will provide information on
the techniques and algorithms that are currently used in real-world computer vision systems
and their applications. It will encourage students to develop new systems based on integrating
machine vision and deep learning.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe the theoretical features and apply the practical aspects of computing with
images
2. Determine the foundation of image formation and image analysis. Explain the basics of
2D and 3D Computer Vision
3. Estimate fundamental perceptions tasks such as image segmentation, object tracking,
and object recognition
4. Summarize some of the key application areas of computer vision

Pre requisite: Nil
Course Objectives
Computer Vision focuses on the development of algorithms and techniques to analyze and
interpret the visible world around us. This requires understanding of the fundamental concepts
related to multi-dimensional signal processing, feature extraction, pattern analysis, visual
geometric modelling, stochastic optimization etc. Knowledge of these concepts is necessary in
this field, to explore and contribute to research and further developments in the field of computer
vision. Applications range from Biometrics, Medical diagnosis, document processing, mining of
visual content, to surveillance, advanced rendering etc. The aim of the course is to familiarize
the students with the fundamental concepts of Computer Vision. It will provide information on
the techniques and algorithms that are currently used in real-world computer vision systems
and their applications. It will encourage students to develop new systems based on integrating
machine vision and deep learning.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe the theoretical features and apply the practical aspects of computing with
images
2. Determine the foundation of image formation and image analysis. Explain the basics of
2D and 3D Computer Vision
3. Estimate fundamental perceptions tasks such as image segmentation, object tracking,
and object recognition
4. Summarize some of the key application areas of computer vision

Pre-requisite: Probability/Python/Programming language/Robotics
Objectives:
1. Robotics is the science of perceiving and manipulating the physical world through
computer-controlled mechanical devices. Examples of successful robotic systems
include mobile platforms for planetary exploration, robotics arms in assembly lines,
cars that travel autonomously on highways, actuated arms that assist surgeons.
2. Robotics systems have in common that they are situated in the physical world, perceive
their environments through sensors, and manipulate their environment through things
that move.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to :
1. Environments. Physical worlds are inherently unpredictable. While the degree of
uncertainty in well-structured environments such assembly lines is small, environments
such as highways and private homes are highly dynamic and unpredictable.
2. Sensors. Sensors are inherently limited in what they can perceive. Limitations arise from
two primary factors. First, range and resolution of a sensor is subject to physical laws. For
example, Cameras can’t see through walls, and even within the perceptual range the
spatial resolution of camera images is limited. Second, sensors are subject to noise, which
perturbs sensor measurements in unpredictable ways and hence limits the information
that can be extracted from sensor measurements.
3. Robots. Robot actuation involves motors that are, at least to some extent, unpredictable,
due effects like control noise and wear-and-tear. Some actuators, such as heavy-duty
industrial robot arms, are quite accurate. Others, like low-cost mobile robots, can be
extremely inaccurate.
4. Models. Models are inherently inaccurate. Models are abstractions of the real world. As
such, they only partially model the underlying physical processes of the robot and its
Signature
(Prepared by Concerned Faculty/HOD)

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
environment. Model errors are a source of uncertainty that has largely been ignored in
robotics, despite the fact that most robotic models used in state-or-the-art robotics systems
are rather crude.
5. Computation. Robots are real-time systems, which limits the amount of computation that
can be carried out. Many state-of-the-art algorithms (such as most of the algorithms
described in this book) are approximate, achieving timely response through sacrificing
accuracy.

Pre-requisite: Probability/Python/Programming language/Robotics
Objectives:
Robotics is the science of perceiving and manipulating the physical world through computer-
controlled mechanical devices. Examples of successful robotic systems include mobile platforms for
planetary exploration, robotics arms in assembly lines, cars that travel autonomously on highways,
actuated arms that assist surgeons.
Robotics systems have in common that they are situated in the physical world, perceive their
environments through sensors, and manipulate their environment through things that move.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to :
1. Environments. Physical worlds are inherently unpredictable. While the degree of uncertainty in
well-structured environments such assembly lines is small, environments such as highways and
private homes are highly dynamic and unpredictable.
2. Sensors. Sensors are inherently limited in what they can perceive. Limitations arise from two
primary factors. First, range and resolution of a sensor is subject to physical laws. For example,
Cameras can’t see through walls, and even within the perceptual range the spatial resolution of
camera images is limited. Second, sensors are subject to noise, which perturbs sensor
measurements in unpredictable ways and hence limits the information that can be extracted from
sensor measurements.
3. Robots. Robot actuation involves motors that are, at least to some extent, unpredictable, due effects
like control noise and wear-and-tear. Some actuators, such as heavy-duty industrial robot arms,
are quite accurate. Others, like low-cost mobile robots, can be extremely inaccurate.
4. Models. Models are inherently inaccurate. Models are abstractions of the real world. As such, they
only partially model the underlying physical processes of the robot and its environment. Model
errors are a source of uncertainty that has largely been ignored in robotics, despite the fact that
most robotic models used in state-or-the-art robotics systems are rather crude.
5. Computation. Robots are real-time systems, which limits the amount of computation that can be
carried out. Many state-of-the-art algorithms (such as most of the algorithms described in this
book) are approximate, achieving timely response through sacrificing accuracy.

Pre-requisite: Probability / Python/ Programming language/ Robotics

Objectives:

Robotics is the science of perceiving and manipulating the physical world through
computer-controlled mechanical devices. Examples of successful robotic systems include
mobile platforms for planetary exploration, robotics arms in assembly lines, cars that travel
autonomously on highways, actuated arms that assist surgeons.

Robotics systems have in common that they are situated in the physical world, perceive

their environments through sensors, and manipulate their environment through things that
move.

Outcomes:

After completion of the course, students would be able to :

1. Environments. Physical worlds are inherently unpredictable. While the degree of
uncertainty in well-structured environments such assembly lines is small, environments
such as highways and private homes are highly dynamic and unpredictable.

2. Sensors. Sensors are inherently limited in what they can perceive. Limitations arise
from two primary factors. First, range and resolution of a sensor is subject to physical
laws. For example, Cameras can’t see through walls, and even within the perceptual
range the spatial resolution of camera images is limited. Second, sensors are subject to
noise, which perturbs sensor measurements in unpredictable ways and hence limits the
information that can be extracted from sensor measurements.

3. Robots. Robot actuation involves motors that are, at least to some extent, unpredictable,
due effects like control noise and wear-and-tear. Some actuators, such as heavy-duty
industrial robot arms, are quite accurate. Others, like low-cost mobile robots, can be
extremely inaccurate.

4. Models. Models are inherently inaccurate. Models are abstractions of the real world. As
such, they only partially model the underlying physical processes of the robot and its
environment. Model errors are a source of uncertainty that has largely been ignored in
robotics, despite the fact that most robotic models used in state-or-the-art robotics
systems are rather crude.

5. Computation. Robots are real-time systems, which limits the amount of computation
that can be carried out. Many state-of-the-art algorithms (such as most of the algorithms

described in this book) are approximate, achieving timely response through sacrificing
accuracy.

Pre-requisite: NIL
Course Objective
The Seminar course is designed to enhance the students' presentation and research skills. It provides
students an opportunity to explore contemporary topics in data science, conduct an in-depth literature
review, and present their findings to an academic audience. The seminar aims to develop critical
thinking, oral communication, and the ability to engage with technical discussions.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Identify and evaluate recent advancements or research trends in a chosen domain of data science
through comprehensive literature review.
2. Develop and deliver clear, concise technical presentations with effective oral communication
skills.
3. Synthesize research findings into a structured, well-documented technical report.
4. Demonstrate the ability to address technical questions and engage in meaningful discussions
during presentations.
Detailed Syllabus
The students of a group would contact the concerned faculty to find a mutually convenient 2 hour/
week schedule for the seminar course. The group would be required to meet their faculty instructor
regularly and seek advice on the topic of the seminar and guidance in various aspects of technical
presentation (Example: Composition of presentation, Length of presentation, Graphical Vs textual
aspects, Content density, etc.) The organization of the course can be divided into two parts. The initial
phase includes the students deciding seminar topics and receiving guidance on technical
communication aspects. This could also include mock presentations which could facilitate faculty and
peer feedback. The second part of the seminar course would include student presentations, spread over
several sessions; based on which grade is awarded.

privacy, data ownership and responsible AI. Students will learn to integrate ethical considerations into

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till first year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year students’
learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate with the required
practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think critically, solve challenging problems,
do a feasibility study and develop written and oral communication skills, teamwork, and planning. The
students may also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope and learning in
different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Identify and select an appropriate problem statement through comprehensive literature review and
recognition of research gaps.
2. Formulate multiple use cases and feasible design models based on the selected problem.
3. Plan the project workflow by allocating tasks, resources, and timelines effectively within a team
environment.
4. Implement the prototype or proof of concept and systematically test and validate the results.
5. Demonstrate teamwork, leadership, and collaboration skills while managing a project.
6. Summarize the research work in a structured technical report and deliver an effective oral
presentation.
Detailed Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design and fabrication
work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and verify feasibility of
implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to submit a report detailing the literature
review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and synthesis, work plan and work done
and present his/her work carried out before examiners.
